source.title: Transformers are uninterpretable with myopic methods: a case study with bounded Dyck grammars
source.authors: Kai-Yue Wen; Yu-Chen Li; Bing Liu; Andrej Risteski

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies Transformer solutions and generalization on bounded Dyck grammars, but does not test grokking's delayed-generalization pattern or the other listed grokking versions. It cites work on grokking-related progress measures without testing that claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Dyck-task accuracy and length-generalization results, but no training-accuracy/test-accuracy trajectory, overfitting delay, or training-set-size sweep. Its attention-pattern variation results are not measurements of the grokking claims and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study trains small Transformers on bounded Dyck grammars to show that individual attention patterns or weights do not reveal the algorithm. It reports no train/test accuracy trajectories, no delay after overfitting, no training-set-size sweep, no progress measures and no weight-decay or optimizer manipulation of a generalization delay. Grokking work (Nanda et al. 2023, Zhong et al. 2023) is only cited, so it tests none of V1–V7. Its across-seed attention-variation result touches V6's question of whether runs converge to the same solution. But it measures variation in single attention heads, not identity of the algorithm. The authors say circuit-level understanding remains possible, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Transformers on Dyck implement a rich set of solutions whose individual attention patterns or weights need not reflect task structure, so myopic interpretability is insufficient. They also find that balance regularization improves length generalization. They state this does not contradict circuit-level mechanistic interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Transformers on bounded Dyck grammar next-token prediction and evaluates attention patterns and length generalization; it does not reproduce a grokking experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that attention patterns vary with embedding choice, positional encoding, random initialization, and learning rate. Contrastive regularization changes balance violation and length-generalization performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Second-layer attention patterns differ widely across random seeds, embeddings, positional encodings and learning rates, despite ≥97% accuracy. Mean variation is 2.20 and 2.27 against a random baseline of 2.85, and 0.24 with a minimal first layer (Sec 4.1, Table 1). Theory shows many non-stack-like attention patterns, including uniform attention, solve Dyck.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformers trained on the same algorithmic task (Dyck) reach functionally equivalent solutions whose individual attention patterns vary nearly as much as random patterns across seeds and hyperparameters. This is related to V6, but it measures component variation, not algorithm identity.

fits_no_version.finding: Contrastive regularization for balanced attention reduces balance violation and improves length generalization (Fig 3, Fig 10). In-distribution accuracy is ≥97% for all models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On bounded Dyck, regularizing for the balance condition improves length generalization of 2-layer Transformers.

record.problems: The reported length-generalization accuracies in the relevant figures are not stated numerically in the text. The study does not measure delayed generalization after overfitting or compare delays across training-set sizes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the grokking versions. Attention-variation results and their random baselines are outside the listed claims.

untested.parts: delayed test-accuracy jump after training saturation; delay vs training-set size
gradual circuit formation, memorization cleanup, progress measures anticipating the jump
non-algorithmic data; initialization scale or weight norm switching delays
weight-decay efficiency account, critical dataset size, ungrokking (Corollary 2 on weight decay concerns balance, not grokking)
whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm (only attention-pattern variation is measured)
optimizer or numerical artifacts producing delay

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/cites_only is correct. The attention-variation numbers were left out of the rows. They are recorded under fits_no_version because they concern solution diversity across runs, a construct adjacent to V6, but they measure single-head attention, not algorithm identity.

rows.subject: Transformers trained on Dyck (aggregate: all models)
rows.size_stated: two-layer models: hidden dimension 50 and embedding dimension 50
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate prediction accuracy on held-out in-distribution prefixes ending with a closing bracket
rows.measure: Accuracy at predicting the last bracket from the rest of the prefix
rows.note: The result is stated for all models collectively; no per-model values are given. It does not report a delayed rise after overfitting.
rows.check: This is an in-distribution capability check (≥97% accuracy for all models), not a result on any grokking version. It is a training-outcome threshold, not a comparison with a baseline.

source_check.correct: All models achieve ≥97% in-distribution last-closing-bracket prediction accuracy. For grokking, state=cannot_determine; versions=none.
source_check.problem: Observed describes task accuracy here; this measure cannot establish any grokking version.

rows.subject: Transformers with a minimal first layer and embedding 19
rows.operation_detail: Measure length-generalization accuracy after default training
rows.note: The text says standard training has high balance violations that negatively correlate with length-generalization performance, but gives no exact accuracy value.
rows.check: The value is figure-only and is the baseline arm of the contrastive-regularization comparison. It is the study's own method comparison and bears on no version.

rows.subject: Transformers with a minimal first layer and embedding 19
rows.operation_detail: Train with contrastive regularization intended to reduce balance violation
rows.value: figure only; the text reports improved length-generalization performance
rows.note: The authors report that contrastive regularization reduces balance violation and improves length generalization; exact accuracy values are not stated.
rows.check: This compares the study's own proposed regularizer against standard training, read from figures only. It bears on no grokking version.

source_check.problem: The study's own regularizer comparison does not measure a grokking effect and should not serve as a claim-evidence row.

relation.reason: Nanda et al. is cited as circuit-level interpretability work; grokking is not experimentally investigated or used.

tranche.reason: The study examines Dyck attention patterns and length generalization; it neither tests nor uses grokking.

source_check.notes: Diverse attention patterns do not establish different identifiable algorithms across runs, so they do not directly test V6. R1–R3 are capability or method-comparison results, not evidence for a grokking version.
